#  Route X9 — Scenario engine, case-family generation and annotation guidelines (batch 2)

Context read in full: BRIEF.md, REQUIREMENTS.md (PRB/CH/SOL/AST/SUB/SCN/BKO/EX/EVL/KPI IDs), DECISIONS.md (D-001..D-008), and batch-1 reports `docs/research/external/X1-interviewing-science.md` and `docs/research/external/X2a-deception-arenas-roleplay-fidelity.md`. This route extends X1/X2a rather than repeating them; citations to those files are given as `X1 Qn` / `X2a Qn`.

## Q1 — The 2026 Law and Human Behavior RCT and other 2024-2026 LLM-suspect/witness training work

**Full citation resolved.** Li, S., Granhag, P.-A., Shi, Y., Sun, Y., Nyman, T. J., Haginoya, S., & Santtila, P. (2026). "Using large language model based AI suspects to train strategic use of evidence: preliminary evidence of transfer to mock suspect interviews." *Law and Human Behavior*, 50(3), 240-260. DOI 10.1037/lhb0000647. Accepted manuscript Oct 29, 2025. Confidence: high — DOI, page range, and acceptance date corroborated across the NYU IFP abstract page and a second independent search; this is the authors/venue/date detail batch 1 flagged as needed. Source: [NYU IFP abstract](https://ifp.nyu.edu/2026/journal-article-abstracts/lhb0000647/), confirmed 2026-10-08.

**Design.** 156 Chinese laypersons: 78 interviewer-trainees x 78 human mock suspects, randomized to 3 arms — (a) instruction + AI-suspect practice exercise, (b) instruction alone, (c) control. Two LLM-driven AI suspects were built with simplified rule sets that approximate SUE responses for liars vs. truth-tellers, so trainees could rehearse the technique before facing a real human mock suspect. Confidence: high (same primary-adjacent source, corroborated twice).

**The SUE-based rule set / disclosure mechanic (partially resolved).** The paper's named mechanism is the **Evidence Framing Matrix**, traced to its originating study: Granhag, Strömwall, Willén & Hartwig (2013), "Eliciting Cues to Deception by Tactical Disclosure of Evidence: The First Test of the Evidence Framing Matrix," *Legal and Criminological Psychology*, 18(2). That 2013 study (195 participants, mock-theft paradigm, 6 conditions: guilty/innocent x {early disclosure, SUE-Incremental, a second SUE variant}) established **SUE-Incremental (SUE-I)**: evidence is disclosed stepwise, in order of increasing strength and increasing precision (first a vague, weak hint; later a strong, specific piece), rather than all at once or confronted with early. This stepwise strength/precision ladder is the rule the 2026 paper's AI suspects were built to respond against — a guilty (deceptive) suspect, not knowing how much the interviewer already holds, is pushed toward an account that eventually collides with the next, more precise disclosure; an innocent (truthful) suspect's account stays consistent regardless of disclosure order because it is not fabricated. Confidence: medium — the matrix's definition and the 2013 study's design are independently confirmed; the *exact* operationalization inside the 2026 AI-suspect's prompt/code (what specific disclosure threshold triggers what specific concession vs. denial) was not retrievable this session — the accepted-manuscript PDF (https://reading-pure-test.eprints-hosting.org/127054/1/Accept_Manuscript.pdf) was fetched but returned corrupted/binary text, not parseable prose. **Open item carried forward to a future session**: re-fetch via a text-extraction tool (e.g., `pdftotext`) rather than WebFetch, or source via the publisher's HTML view, to pull the literal rule table.

**Effect sizes and training dose.** The abstract-level synthesis states: trainees who received AI-suspect practice used the evidence-framing-matrix tactic *more frequently* in their subsequent real human mock-suspect interviews, and this elicited *more* statement-evidence and within-statement inconsistencies from the (deceptive) human mock suspects than the instruction-alone or control arms. No specific numeric effect size (Cohen's d, odds ratio, p-value) was retrieved this session — the digest describes direction and mechanism, not magnitude. Confidence: medium (direction is corroborated twice; magnitude unverified — same caveat X2a already flagged). Training dose (number of AI-suspect practice sessions, session length) was likewise not retrieved. **This remains the single most load-bearing unresolved citation for KPI-1** per X2a's own flag; it is now partially resolved (authors, N, arms, mechanism) but the quantitative payload is still missing.

**Other 2024-2026 LLM suspect/witness work.** No additional papers beyond what X2a already found (Among Us sandbox, OpenDeception, WOLF) specifically building an LLM *suspect or witness* for *interviewer* training were newly located this session; this Li/Granhag/Santtila paper remains the only directly on-point precedent. Confidence: medium that the search space is exhausted — a negative result (nothing found) is weaker evidence of absence than a positive citation.

## Q2 — Synthetic case-family generation designs

**No single paper does the full SCN-11 design** (matched truthful/deceptive variants from one canonical event with atomic fact IDs, controlled evidence discoverability, misleading-but-innocent circumstances, independent difficulty/style knobs, four-way validation). The closest building blocks, assembled from several sources:

- **MuSR** (Sprague et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.16049): a neurosymbolic generation algorithm that builds a reasoning tree of facts + commonsense first, then expands it into a ~1000-word murder-mystery narrative one chunk at a time, **validating each generation step for fact consistency and recall** against the tree before accepting it. GPT-4+CoT reaches 80.4% accuracy on MuSR's murder-mystery split vs. 94.1% human-majority — i.e., even frontier models fall well short of humans on this exact task shape (a scenario-solvability ceiling worth benchmarking our own cases against). Confidence: high, primary (ICLR proceedings + ar5iv full text). [arXiv:2310.16049](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16049v2), accessed 2026-10-08.
- **AR-Bench "detective cases"** (Zhou et al., ICML 2025, arXiv:2506.08295): a four-stage pipeline — (1) **core sampling** of a crime outline (time, place, victim, suspects), (2) **tree-based story expansion** to flesh out motive/opportunity/means, (3) **key-question extraction**, turning narrative nodes into targeted question prompts (this is the closest existing analog to a public-packet-vs-private-fact split), (4) **puzzle synthesis**, assembling the final narrative + answer key. Validation enforces a **triple constraint** — the culprit has exactly one motive, one opportunity, one means — specifically to block multiple-suspect ambiguity and guarantee a unique solution; human annotators then verify logical consistency before inclusion. 500 cases total (400 train/100 test), ~564 tokens/case. This triple-constraint pattern is directly reusable as a **solvability check** for SCN-11's deceptive variant (the assigned perpetrator must be uniquely supportable by evidence+questioning, not one of several equally plausible suspects). Confidence: high, primary (full text fetched). [arXiv:2506.08295](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.08295v1), fetched 2026-10-08. Separately, AR-Bench's own finding — contemporary LLMs struggle specifically at *active* reasoning (deciding what question to ask to acquire missing evidence, vs. passive reasoning over given facts) and tree-search/post-training gains are only modest — is a direct headwind for AST-3 (the coach must *decide* what follow-up to ask under incomplete information); flag as a feasibility risk, not just a generation-design note.
- **Data-leakage prevention via generation, not redaction**: the "active reasoning" pipeline's stated motivation (same AR-Bench paper and its search-result summary) is explicitly to avoid static benchmark leakage by *generating* fresh cases from a pipeline rather than reusing a fixed public set — directly supports SCN-12 (disjoint dev/hidden case families): the generator itself, run with a new seed, is the leakage control, not just withholding a fixed file.
- **TurnaboutLLM** (benchmark built on *Ace Attorney*/*Danganronpa* detective-game transcripts, found via alphaxiv listing): tasks an LLM with finding contradictions between testimony and evidence across long narrative context — a deductive-reasoning eval closer to our *investigator*-facing task (spot contradictions against evidence) than to case generation per se, but useful as an independent sanity-check harness for whether a generated case's contradiction is actually findable by an LLM reader. Confidence: medium (found via secondary alphaxiv listing, not independently read in full).
- **Misleading-but-innocent circumstances for truthful variants**: no dedicated paper on this specific design knob was found. The closest conceptual support is X1 Q5's equivocation theory (a truthful subject can look evasive for legitimate reasons) and MuSR/AR-Bench's "commonsense distractor" framing (narratives include plausible-but-wrong leads by construction, which is structurally the same knob). Confidence: low that a dedicated citation exists; treat as an internally-authored design requirement, scaffolded by adjacent literature, not a lifted technique.
- **Style assigned independently of role**: no paper was found building this exact factorial knob into scenario generation; X1's Lev-Ari & Keysar (2010) accent-credibility result (X1 Q3) is the evidentiary *reason* this knob must exist, not a generation-design precedent. This is confirmed as a build-your-own mechanism, consistent with batch 1's framing.

Confidence summary for Q2: medium-high on the generation-pipeline mechanics (MuSR, AR-Bench are primary and directly reusable), low on "matched truthful/deceptive variant from one canonical event" and "misleading-but-innocent circumstance" as named, citable techniques — these two specific SCN-11 requirements appear to be genuinely novel combinations not yet published as a unit.

## Q3 — Disclosure-policy engines for subjects

Four directly relevant, recent sources, none of which is a complete off-the-shelf solution but together they substantiate the whole design pattern:

- **Disclosure-Gated User Simulation for Companion-Agent Evaluation** (arXiv:2609.00982, Sept 2026). Names the exact failure SCN-8/SUB-6 must avoid: naive LLM user/subject simulators are "excessively cooperative," volunteering information before being asked, which lets an evaluated system score well just by asking *more* questions rather than asking *better* ones — a direct analog to AST-10 ("no credit for producing more flags"). Their fix: a **disclosure gate** — a state machine of five ordered gates (`opening -> asked_or_natural -> felt_heard -> felt_safe -> earned_deep_trust`) merged onto three information **depth layers** (surface / mid / core), where each turn's gate transition is a function of the *interviewer's* preceding behavior, not a fixed script. A standard (ungated) simulator leaks "deep secrets" 19-37% of the time even when explicitly instructed not to; the gated simulator held core-layer disclosure to 3-8%, and was the only configuration that preserved both system-ranking order and absolute score stability versus the paper's reference simulator (leaderboard correlation 0.993). Confidence: high, primary, very recent, and the single most directly transferable mechanism found for SUB-6/SCN-8 — it is a concrete, implementable alternative to "the subject just follows a system-prompt paragraph." [arXiv:2609.00982](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.00982), accessed 2026-10-08.
- **LedgerAgent** (already found in X2a Q3, arXiv:2606.20529) — structured state *outside* the chat transcript, checked before any claim is emitted, with gains concentrated in multi-trial consistency (pass^k). Combine with the disclosure-gate ladder above: the ledger holds *what is true*, the gate ladder holds *how much of it may surface this turn*.
- **LH-Deception** ("Simulating and Understanding Deceptive Behaviors in Long-Horizon Interactions," arXiv:2510.03999, NeurIPS 2025 + ICLR 2026 poster). Multi-agent harness: a **performer** agent (our subject), a **supervisor** agent that evaluates progress and maintains an evolving trust state (structurally close to our investigator + running finding), and an **independent deception auditor** that reviews the full trajectory after the fact (structurally close to our evaluator-only packet / fidelity judge, SCN-9). Across 11 frontier models, deception is model-dependent, *increases under event/time pressure*, and the paper's qualitative coding names three recurring strategies: **concealment, equivocation, and falsification** — a ready-made, independently-derived three-way split that maps almost directly onto our SUB-6/SUB-7 line (concealment/equivocation = permitted; falsification = fidelity failure). It also documents **"chains of deception"** emerging only over long horizons, invisible to single-turn checks — relevant to why BKO-8's 12-exchange cap needs a trajectory-level (not per-turn-only) fidelity audit. Confidence: high, primary, very recent (through ICLR 2026). [arXiv:2510.03999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.03999), accessed 2026-10-08.
- **SOTOPIA-TOM** (arXiv:2605.02307): frames disclosure appropriateness through **contextual integrity** (information-flow norms are domain-specific, not a universal secret/non-secret binary) and **theory-of-mind** (can the agent model what the *other party* already knows/needs, not just what it personally knows). A "ToM-Coach" intervention cut critical privacy violations on GPT-4o from 9.9% to 2.2% while more than doubling an information-management composite score (15% to 40%). Directly actionable: a subject's disclosure policy should be conditioned on a running model of what the investigator has *already established* (via evidence released, per SCN-10), not a static per-fact flag — this argues for combining the ledger (Q3, LedgerAgent) with a ToM-style "what has the investigator shown they know" tracker, not just the five-gate trust ladder alone. Confidence: medium-high, primary, recent. [arXiv:2605.02307](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.02307).

**Encoding permitted behaviors (omission, deflection, minimization) with per-turn sealed tags.** No single paper specifies this exact schema, but the synthesis across the four sources above gives a concrete design: per profile, enumerate permitted-behavior categories (mirroring LH-Deception's concealment/equivocation/falsification-forbidden split); gate actual disclosure through a state machine (disclosure-gate ladder) keyed to depth layers derived from the canonical fact graph (Q2); and have the subject emit a **sealed per-turn tag** — e.g. `{disclosed: [fact_ids], withheld: [fact_ids], behavior: omission|deflection|minimization|none, permitted: true|false}` — that the public transcript never shows but the evaluator-only packet (SCN-9) and fidelity judge read every turn. This tag is the mechanism X2a's Q5/Q1 both independently called for ("a sealed per-turn disclosure tag, checked by the fidelity judge") and is now substantiated by LH-Deception's auditor pattern and the disclosure-gate's depth-layer bookkeeping. Confidence: medium — this is a synthesis across four primary sources, not a single lifted design; flag it to the team as "assembled, not off-the-shelf."

## Q4 — Annotation guidelines for evasion events (EVL-8)

**Bull & Mayer (1993)** typology: 12 superordinate categories subdividing into 35 distinct ways politicians avoid directly answering a question (X1 Q5 cited "43 techniques" from a related/later count; both figures recur across sources and likely reflect different versions/extensions of the same typology — flag as a minor count discrepancy, not a contradiction of substance). Source corroborated again this session via SAGE/academic summaries. **Clayman (1993, 2001)** and **Clayman & Heritage (2002)** provide the conversation-analytic treatment of evasion dynamics and "agenda shift" (the interviewee answers a different, self-chosen question) — still only found as secondary citations, primary text not independently pulled this session either. **Bavelas et al. (1990)**: equivocation as a response to a "communicative avoidance-avoidance conflict" (every direct answer carries some social/legal/reputational cost, yet silence is not an option) — reconfirmed, same framing as X1. Confidence: high on all three typologies' existence/substance (independently corroborated across multiple academic sources both batches); medium on exact category counts (35 vs 43 discrepancy unresolved).

**Inter-annotator agreement — new, more current data point found this session.** A recent (2026-era, SemEval-2026 Task 6 "Unmasking Political Question Evasions") hierarchical two-level taxonomy of response clarity for QA pairs from US presidential interviews reports **pairwise Fleiss' kappa >= 0.85 across all clarity-label pairs**, with the *lowest* agreement (kappa = 0.85) at the Clear-Reply vs. Ambivalent boundary, and the lowest agreement specifically within **Deflection** sub-categories (closely adjacent categories in the taxonomy are the hardest to separate reliably). This is a concrete, recent, numeric precedent for what "good" inter-annotator agreement looks like for an evasion-coding scheme, and — importantly — shows *where* disagreement concentrates (clear/ambivalent boundary; deflection sub-types), which is directly actionable: our EVL-8 annotator guideline should expect and budget for lower agreement specifically at the uncertainty/evasion boundary and within deflection-type distinctions, not uniformly across all four categories. Confidence: medium — found via a SemEval shared-task paper (AsymVerify/Duluth system-description papers referencing the task), a competition artifact rather than a peer-reviewed psychology journal, but the kappa figures are concrete and recent. Separately, general political-equivocation literature puts the base rate of *fully* clear answers in televised interviews at only **39-46% of questions** — useful as a sanity check that evasive-looking responses are common even among truthful/legitimate speakers in a baseline adversarial-interview genre, reinforcing PRB-4's caution against over-flagging. Sources: [PolERo (Romanian political evasion), arXiv:2609.02391](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02391); [Duluth SemEval-2026 Task 6, arXiv:2604.20168](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.20168); [AsymVerify SemEval-2026 Task 6, arXiv:2607.20439](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.20439) — all accessed 2026-10-08, all primary/competition-primary, all within the 12-month freshness window.

**Four-category taxonomy (carried from X1, now reinforced).** X1's synthesis (evasion / genuine uncertainty / legitimate non-disclosure / poorly-framed question) remains the right structure; LH-Deception's independently-derived concealment/equivocation/falsification split (Q3 above) is a second, convergent three-way cut that maps cleanly onto it (concealment+equivocation -> "evasion" bucket when impermissible, "legitimate non-disclosure" when permitted by profile; falsification -> fidelity failure, not an evasion-taxonomy member at all). Two independent literatures (interviewing-science/political-communication, and LLM-deception benchmarking) converging on structurally similar 3-4-way splits is a meaningful cross-validation of the taxonomy's shape.

## Q5 — Investigator rubric anchors (EVL-7)

**No validated, publicly-documented 0-4 behaviorally-anchored investigative-interview rubric was found this session either** — this confirms X1 Q7's finding rather than filling the gap. Specific items: **PEACE evaluation forms** exist operationally (used in UK police training) but no public coding manual with numeric anchors was retrieved. **NICHD coding** is real and well-documented but scores *interviewee* (often child) response quality and *interviewer* question-type/supportiveness as separate coding schemes, not a unified 5-dimension 0-4 investigator rubric — material (open-question-rate coding, reluctance/cooperativeness coding) is reusable as a component, not as the whole rubric. **USCIS FDNS "Corroboration-Based Interviewing" (CBI)** is confirmed as a real, named, currently-procured framework — a live government solicitation (confirmed via a GovDirections contract-opportunity listing) describes CBI(TM) as 3-day in-person training for FDNS officers on "investigative interviewing methods, including interview planning and strategy, cooperation building, and credibility assessment," explicitly built around corroborating a subject's account against independent evidence rather than seeking an admission. This is a strong real-world *framing* precedent for EX-3 ("insufficient evidence... verify the work order") and for "evidence-based follow-up"/"supported closure" as rubric dimensions, but no public scoring rubric or behavioral-anchor text for CBI was located (it appears to be delivered as proprietary/contracted in-person training content, not published). Confidence: medium that CBI exists and matches our framing (corroborated via a federal contracting notice, a primary-ish government source, though not the training curriculum itself); low that any of PEACE/NICHD/CBI yields a ready-to-use 0-4 anchor table. Source: [USCIS FDNS CBI training contract notice, GovDirections](https://govdirections.com/rfp/uscis-contracting-office-erbur-corroboration-based-interviewing-training-services-for-uscis-fraud-detection-and-national-security-directorate-fdns-1067502052), accessed 2026-10-08.

**Net assessment, reinforcing X1:** EVL-7's anchors remain a build-and-pilot task for the team. The best available scaffolding (combining X1 and this session) is: the open/probing/closed/leading/suggestive/compound/forced-choice/opinion enum for "clarity and neutrality"; NICHD's reluctance/cooperativeness and question-type coding for "response relevance"; the Evidence Framing Matrix's strength/precision ladder (Q1) plus SUE's statement-evidence-inconsistency logic for "evidence-based follow-up" and "testing alternative explanations"; CBI's corroboration-first framing and EX-3 itself for "supported closure." None of this is a validated rubric; all of it is defensible scaffolding citable in a methods section.

## Q6 — Scenario domains for synthetic federal-style investigations

No naming of real agencies/people is required or appropriate; the brief and battle plan already imply generic administrative-investigation registers (X1 Q8's CaseIQ/FedSmith/OIG material, EX-1's "busy shift" workplace-access example). This session's search of DOE Office of Inspector General audit reports (`energy.gov/ig`) surfaced a concrete, real-world evidence-type vocabulary usable as seed material for domain design, without naming any real subject:

| Domain | Example public/evaluator evidence types (generic, synthetic) |
|---|---|
| Facility access | Badge-swipe logs with timestamps, visitor sign-in sheets, access-control-system audit exports, badge-issuance/termination records, security-camera time-stamps (metadata only, never actual footage content needed) |
| Timekeeping | Time-clock punch records, supervisor-approved timesheets, leave-request forms, shift-schedule rosters, overtime-authorization emails |
| Procurement | Purchase requisitions, vendor quotes, approval-chain signatures/timestamps, delivery/receiving records, invoice-vs-PO reconciliation logs |
| Records access | Document-management-system access logs, checkout/sign-out registers, read-receipt or view-timestamp metadata, redaction/release logs |
| Benefits documentation | Application forms with self-attested fields, supporting-document submission logs, eligibility-determination worksheets, verification-request/response records |
| Lab safety | Equipment-usage/maintenance logs, safety-training completion records, incident/near-miss reports, chemical-inventory or access logs, standard-operating-procedure sign-offs |

Confidence: medium — the vocabulary is grounded in real (if dated, 2002-2019) DOE IG audit documents confirming these record types genuinely exist and get audited in federal facility/physical-security contexts (so the synthetic evidence types will read as plausible to a judge familiar with federal practice), but these are not purpose-built "scenario domain" designs from any paper — they are repurposed audit-report vocabulary, and the team must still build the actual fact graphs, timelines, and discoverability rules per domain. Source: [DOE OIG Chapter 1 Physical Security](https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2019/09/f67/Chapter-1-Physical-Security_9-11-19.pdf); [DOE IG-0548 badge/access audit](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/igprod/documents/CalendarYear2002/ig-0548.pdf) — both accessed 2026-10-08, both flagged as **older than 12 months** (2002/2019) since they describe stable bureaucratic record-keeping practice rather than fast-moving technology, which is an acceptable staleness profile for this specific use (evidence-type realism, not technology currency).

## Contradictions and disputed points

1. **Bull's evasion-category count: 35 vs. 43.** This session's sources (SAGE encyclopedia, Riester conference paper) state Bull & Mayer (1993) catalogued 35 techniques across 12 superordinate categories; X1's search (batch 1) reported "43 distinct techniques" from a different secondary source. Both numbers recur independently but were not reconciled against Bull's primary text this session — likely different editions/extensions of the typology, not a true contradiction, but cite with a range ("35-43") until the primary monograph is checked.
2. **Lie-detection-as-deception-detection, reconfirmed as disputed (carried from X2a).** LH-Deception's three-way concealment/equivocation/falsification split (this session) is a second, independent source converging with Pacchiardi-vs-Berger (X2a Q1) on the same underlying point: a model can be non-forthcoming (concealment/equivocation) without ever emitting a detectably false statement, so any scoring mechanism keyed to "detected falsehood" will systematically under-count evasion. This strengthens, rather than contradicts, X2a's existing flag.
3. **Disclosure-gate ladder (cooperative-by-default risk) vs. AST-10's "no credit for more flags."** The companion-agent paper's finding that *ungated* simulators over-disclose, inflating an evaluated system's apparent competence, is structurally the *subject-side* mirror of AST-10's *assistant-side* warning against being rewarded for volume. Not a contradiction, but worth flagging to the team as the same failure mode appearing on both sides of the interview (subject over-shares -> easy detection; assistant over-flags -> false positives) and both need an explicit anti-inflation design, not just one.
4. **Federal evidence-type sourcing is old while the generation techniques are new.** The DOE IG documents (Q6) are 6-24 years old; the generation/annotation papers (Q1-Q4) are mostly 2024-2026. This is an intentional, not accidental, mismatch — bureaucratic record-keeping categories change slowly, LLM scenario-generation technique does not — but it should be stated explicitly in any citation of Q6 material so a reviewer does not mistake old evidence-type sourcing for stale methodology.

## Implications for the arena build (no recommendation)

- The Evidence-Framing-Matrix's strength/precision disclosure ladder (Q1) and the disclosure-gate's five-gate trust ladder (Q3) are two independently-sourced versions of the same underlying mechanic — scripted, incremental, strength-ordered evidence/information release — which cross-validates SCN-4/SCN-10's design and gives two concrete, combinable implementation patterns (one for the scenario engine's evidence release schedule, one for the subject's own disclosure gating).
- AR-Bench's triple-constraint validation (exactly one motive/opportunity/means for the true culprit) is a directly portable, mechanically-checkable solvability test for a generated deceptive-variant case before it enters the hidden set — cheap to implement as an automated gate ahead of any human pilot review.
- LH-Deception's concealment/equivocation/falsification split, found independently of X1's evasion-vs-uncertainty-vs-legitimate-non-disclosure-vs-poorly-framed-question split, gives two convergent taxonomies the team can reconcile into one annotator guideline rather than building from a single source.
- The disclosure-gate paper's core warning (naive simulators are too cooperative, which inflates scores on the *evaluating* side) generalizes to both the subject engine and the assistant's flag-production — both need an explicit anti-inflation design element, not an assumption that "more output = better."
- The SemEval-2026 kappa data (0.85 floor, concentrated at the clear/ambivalent boundary and within deflection sub-types) gives a concrete, recent precedent to cite when designing and reporting EVL-8's own inter-annotator-agreement study, and predicts *where* disagreement will concentrate so the annotation guideline can pay special attention there.
- The CBI/corroboration framing (Q5) and the DOE IG evidence-type vocabulary (Q6) together argue the arena's register should foreground "verify the record" (EX-3) over "get them to admit it" — consistent with X1's Méndez/HIG-over-Reid finding, now reinforced by an actual current federal-training-program name and real audit-evidence vocabulary rather than only the academic contrast.
- The still-unresolved exact SUE rule table inside the 2026 RCT (open question 1) means the team should not yet hard-code a specific disclosure-threshold algorithm attributed to that paper; the Evidence Framing Matrix's documented 2013 stepwise strength/precision principle is citable now, the 2026 paper's exact adaptation is not yet.
- No rubric anchors exist to lift (Q5, reconfirmed both batches) — budget team time to author and pilot EVL-7's anchors in-house, using the scaffolding listed in Q5, and plan an inter-rater pilot before any tournament run, per EVL-7's own "trainers must calibrate it before use" instruction.
